items.stem: A Massachusetts patient's usual community pharmacy has unexpectedly closed for repairs. The patient urgently needs a Schedule VI maintenance medicine and presents a cell-phone image of an old pharmacy label showing a prior fill. The image does not establish whether a refill remains, and the receiving pharmacist cannot authenticate any prescription or transfer record at that moment. The patient claims that three refills are available. What should the receiving pharmacist do FIRST, without assuming an unverified transfer has occurred?

choices.text: Enter three refills based on the screenshot and tell the patient the pharmacy closure makes the transfer automatic.
choices.why: Incorrect. A patient screenshot alone does not establish the prescriber's authorization or the remaining refill balance.

choices.text: Verify the record and authorization; separately assess lawful continuity options.
choices.why: Correct. The pharmacist must establish legitimate prescription authority and not confuse unverified claims with a completed prescription transfer.

choices.text: Ignore the patient's medication needs until the original pharmacy physically reopens.
choices.why: Incorrect. Continuity and prescriber contact should be evaluated; a closure does not require a blanket refusal to assess lawful options.

choices.text: Create a new annual prescription under the previous prescriber's name without contacting an authorized source.
choices.why: Incorrect. The pharmacist cannot fabricate an original authorization or an annual refill balance.

items.novelty_rationale: Tests verification from an inaccessible pharmacy without relying on the unresolved 2023 Policy 30-day versus 2024 Regulation 14-day duration discrepancy.

items.stem: TRANSFER RECORD — The receiving pharmacist is manually documenting a Schedule IV refill transfer discussed directly with the pharmacist at the old location. The record currently lists the patient and drug, the old pharmacy name, the latest dispensing date, and an assertion that two refills remain. It does NOT show the original prescription issuance date or the name of the pharmacist who performed the transfer. Other legally required transfer information is being collected separately. Which missing information must also be documented? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The patient's credit-card number used at the original pharmacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. Credit-card records are not listed as required transferred prescription information.

choices.text: The original prescription issuance date.
choices.why: Correct. The receiving pharmacist must record the original issuance date for a manual Schedule III-V transfer.

choices.text: A replacement signature from the prescribing physician on every receiving-pharmacy entry.
choices.why: Incorrect. The transfer regulation requires authenticated pharmacist-to-pharmacist information, not an automatic new signature.

choices.text: The name of the pharmacist who transferred the information.
choices.why: Correct. The receiving transfer record must identify the transferring pharmacist.

items.novelty_rationale: A short missing-field audit requires reading a transfer record rather than recognizing a generic definition.

items.stem: A Schedule VI e-prescription says 'take 1 tablet' with no frequency. A properly identified prescriber calls the pharmacist and supplies 'once each morning.' Which statements are appropriate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Document the verified prescriber clarification and incorporate the intended directions before dispensing.
choices.why: Correct. A pharmacist should resolve an incomplete direction with an appropriately authorized source and preserve the corrected order record.

choices.text: Guess a frequency based on the insurance claim's days' supply.
choices.why: Incorrect. Third-party adjudication is not a source of clinical prescriptive authorization.

choices.text: The technician can independently resolve whether the missing frequency should be daily or twice daily.
choices.why: Incorrect. Therapy clarification and professional judgment are not a technician's authorized independent duties.

choices.text: Complete the pharmacist's appropriateness review of the now-clarified prescription before release.
choices.why: Correct. A clarified prescription still requires the pharmacist's prospective DUR and dispensing validation.

items.novelty_rationale: Combines a blank directions field and authenticated prescriber callback without overstating which Schedule II changes are prohibited.

items.stem: A sealed bottle's actual tablets meet specifications, but the manufacturer's label contains a materially false therapeutic claim. Which federal category is established by the false label itself?

choices.text: Adulteration based solely on insanitary manufacturing conditions.
choices.why: Incorrect. The facts do not show insanitary processing or contamination.

choices.text: Adulteration based solely on a different measured drug strength.
choices.why: Incorrect. The tablets are described as meeting specifications, so this ground is not shown.

choices.text: Neither category, because the original seal has not been opened.
choices.why: Incorrect. An intact seal does not excuse materially false drug labeling.

choices.text: Misbranding, because the labeling is false or misleading.
choices.why: Correct. 21 U.S.C. §352(a) identifies false or misleading labeling as a misbranding ground.

items.novelty_rationale: Fills the explicit adulterated-versus-misbranded gap with a product-condition classification that does not incorrectly claim both.

items.stem: An insurer pays a claim, and a patient declines to answer medication-history questions. The pharmacy software still flags a potentially serious interaction on a new prescription. What determines whether it may be released?

choices.text: The paid claim alone, because adjudication certifies that the medicine is clinically safe.
choices.why: Incorrect. Payer adjudication does not replace the pharmacist's prospective DUR.

choices.text: The patient's counseling refusal alone, because it waives evaluation of interaction risk.
choices.why: Incorrect. A counseling decision does not waive the separate pharmacist DUTY to conduct a prospective review.

choices.text: The pharmacist's documented assessment and any appropriate intervention to address the interaction.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.17 requires pharmacist DUR and documentation of measures in response to identified problems.

choices.text: The absence of an allergy listed in the system, even though other profile information is incomplete.
choices.why: Incorrect. A missing allergy entry does not by itself resolve a drug-drug interaction alert.

items.novelty_rationale: Separates a paid claim and counseling refusal from an unresolved prospective DUR concern.

items.stem: Two oral cold products are offered for nonprescription purchase: Product P contains pseudoephedrine; Product F contains phenylephrine but no pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, or phenylpropanolamine. Which one triggers the federal scheduled-listed-chemical retail-sale controls on the stated ingredients?

choices.text: Product P, because pseudoephedrine is a listed chemical with regulated retail-sale conditions.
choices.why: Correct. Federal CMEA controls attach to scheduled-listed chemical products containing pseudoephedrine.

choices.text: Product F, because phenylephrine is handled under the same federal pseudoephedrine sales log requirement.
choices.why: Incorrect. Phenylephrine alone is not one of the listed retail-sale precursors specified in this rule.

choices.text: Both products, because every nasal decongestant is tracked under the same federal precursor rule.
choices.why: Incorrect. Chemical identity, rather than therapeutic category, controls the CMEA scheduled-listed-product classification.

choices.text: Neither product, because nonprescription products cannot trigger a federal sales log.
choices.why: Incorrect. The federal framework specifically regulates qualifying nonprescription sales of scheduled-listed chemical products.

items.novelty_rationale: Tests direct ingredient-level identification rather than memorizing only numeric sale limits.

items.stem: A customer asks for the FDA-approved OTC Narcan 4-mg naloxone nasal spray from a retail shelf and has no prescription. Which is the correct initial classification of this transaction?

choices.text: It is Schedule II dispensing because naloxone acts at opioid receptors.
choices.why: Incorrect. Naloxone is not a controlled substance; receptor pharmacology does not define its controlled schedule.

choices.text: Sell the approved OTC product without requiring a new individual prescription.
choices.why: Correct. FDA approved Narcan 4-mg nasal spray for nonprescription sale; its OTC status does not depend on a new individual prescription.

choices.text: It must be entered as a refill of the customer's previous opioid prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. A naloxone purchase is not a refill of the original opioid prescription.

choices.text: It is a valid OTC sale only after an individual DEA-registered practitioner signs a new paper prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. FDA's specific OTC approval eliminates a general prescription prerequisite for that presentation.

items.citation: FDA Narcan OTC approval Mar. 29, 2023; 247 CMR 9.06; M.G.L. c.94C §19C
items.novelty_rationale: Tests approved dosage-form-specific OTC classification and separates a retail sale from a prescription-paid claim.

qa_note: C070 deliberately avoids disputed duration claim from older 2023 Board Policy vs current 247 CMR 9.04(12); requires final source/source-interpretation audit before exam use.
